title: Pressure-cooker steel-cut oats
subtitle: Nutty, chewy porridge in 10 minutes instead of 30
excerpt: Steel-cut oats cooked under pressure into a thick, satisfying porridge. The method compresses a 30-minute stovetop cook to 10 minutes under pressure, with none of the stirring required.
sourceNotes: Steel-cut oats (pinhead or Irish oats) are oat groats cut with steel blades rather than rolled. They have more texture and nuttiness than rolled oats and traditionally take 30 minutes of stovetop cooking. The pressure-cooker method compresses this significantly.

recipe.batchNotes: Cook a large batch, cool, and refrigerate in individual portions for up to 5 days. Reheat with a splash of milk.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Reheat in a saucepan or microwave with a splash of water or milk.

content.text: Steel-cut oats have a coarser texture and nuttier flavour than rolled oats. They hold their shape in the finished porridge rather than turning into a paste. The pressure cooker cuts 30 minutes of stovetop stirring to about 10 minutes. The result has the chew that makes steel-cut oats worth cooking.

Do not substitute rolled oats in this recipe, they cook much faster and will become overcooked mush in the same time. For rolled oats, see the rolled oat oatmeal entry. Use porridge oats, the coarser, traditional Scottish style, for the best texture here.
As with all oat porridges cooked under pressure, foam is an issue. Do not fill more than half the pot, and always use natural pressure release.

Put the porridge oats, {{whole-milk}} of whole milk, 500 ml of water, and salt into the pressure cooker. Stir briefly to combine. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 10 minutes. Allow a full natural pressure release, this takes about 10 minutes. Never quick-release oatmeal.

Open the lid and stir vigorously to combine, the porridge will have separated slightly and needs stirring back together. If too thick, stir in a splash of warm milk. Taste and add a pinch of salt. Serve with honey, cream, or fresh fruit.

rows.symptom: Foam or porridge came from the valve during cooking
rows.cause: The pot was more than half full, or quick-release was attempted.
rows.fix: Never fill the pot more than halfway for oats. Always use natural pressure release for porridge, it takes 10 minutes but is non-negotiable.

rows.cause: A greater liquid-to-oat ratio was used than the recipe requires.
rows.fix: Simmer in the open pot over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring constantly, to reduce to the desired consistency.

rows.cause: Steel-cut oats are meant to be chewy, this is the characteristic texture.
rows.fix: If a smoother result is preferred, cook for 12 minutes at pressure next time. For fully smooth porridge, rolled oats are a better choice.

content.text: Steel-cut oat porridge is a thoroughly northern breakfast, Scottish and Irish in origin, warming, and very slow to release energy through the morning. The pressure cooker removes the half-hour stovetop commitment that has always been the argument against it on a weekday. Serve simply, as the traditional method dictates: a pinch of salt, a pool of cold milk poured around the edge, and nothing else if you are being orthodox.
